n: Hiram, king of the Phoenician city of Tyre, sends envoys to congratulate Solomon. He had been a long-time friend and ally of David.

f.g: A loyal ally; “love” was treaty language for faithful friendship between kings.

n: Solomon responds with a proposal of his own.
He explains that David could not build the temple because of constant wars. Chronicles adds that David had shed much blood, so God reserved the task for a man of peace.

f.w: under the soles of his feet
f.g: Completely subdued, an image of total victory.

n: Now God has given Solomon peace on every side, with no enemy or disaster to distract him. Peace is the right setting for building a house of God.
Solomon announces his plan to build a temple for the Lord’s name, fulfilling God’s promise to David that his son would do so.

f.w: an house unto the name of the LORD
f.g: God’s “name” stands for His presence, authority, and character.

f.w: he shall build an house unto my name

n: He asks Hiram to have cedars cut in Lebanon, offering to pay the workers. The Phoenicians were the ancient world’s finest timber craftsmen.

f.g: The cedars of Lebanon were prized for their size, durability, and fragrance.
Phoenicians; Sidon and Tyre were their main cities.

n: Hiram rejoices and praises the Lord for giving David such a wise son. Even this foreign king recognizes Israel’s God and Solomon’s wisdom.

f.w: Blessed be the LORD this day

n: Hiram agrees to supply all the cedar and fir (or cypress) timber Solomon wants.
His men will haul the logs to the coast, tie them into rafts, and float them south to Solomon’s chosen port. In exchange Hiram asks for food for his household.

f.w: the place that thou shalt appoint
f.g: Chronicles names Joppa, the port nearest Jerusalem.

n: Hiram provides all the cedar and cypress Solomon needs.
Solomon pays with large annual shipments of wheat and pressed olive oil. Phoenicia, a narrow coastal land, depended on Israel’s farmland for food.

f.g: Measures = kors; a very large amount of grain.

n: God keeps His promise of wisdom, seen in the peace and treaty Solomon forms with Hiram.
Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelite men into forced labor for the project.
They work in rotating shifts — one month in Lebanon, two months home — under Adoniram’s supervision. Still, this burden would later cause resentment.
Seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters work in the hills. Chronicles indicates many were non-Israelite residents of the land.
Thirty-three hundred foremen supervise the workers.
Large, costly, carefully dressed stones are quarried for the temple’s foundation. The house of the Lord was to rest on the finest foundation.
Israelite and Phoenician craftsmen, including masons from Gebal, work together to prepare timber and stone. Israelites and foreigners join in building God’s house.

f.g: Hebrew Giblim — men of Gebal (Byblos), a Phoenician city famous for stonework.
